newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Southeast Asian cocoa producers plan cartel.
newsitem.headline: Southeast Asian cocoa producers plan cartel.

text.p: Southeast Asian cocoa producers plan to set up a regional cartel to help insulate them against global price volatility, government and trade sources said on Tuesday.

Details of the "Single ASEAN Contract" project, proposed and being coordinated by Malaysia, were sketchy but the sources said the Philippines and Thailand had expressed an interest in the move while Indonesia was undecided.
An Indonesian government official said the agriculture ministry was preparing to host a regional meeting in March in Jakarta when the cartel proposal would be explored in detail.
"We have invited officials and industry groups from ASEAN to attend the March meeting," the official told Reuters. "Officials from Cambodia, Laos and Burma would also be invited."
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) groups Brunei, Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Cambodia, Laos and Burma are awaiting formal entry.
"The idea is to allow ASEAN cocoa producers to speak with one voice," the official said.
"But there are several things that needed to be sorted out, such as the quality of beans and cocoa butter, common pricing and if the private sector will agree," the official said.
He said the project was in the formative stage and that no target date had been set.
Recent attempts at commodity cartels have failed worldwide with only rubber controlled by a pact to stabilise prices.
"The eventual aim of the project is to make ASEAN look like it is one big seller, with the same price and quality...putting it in a better bargaining position," the official said.
Indonesia is the world's third largest cocoa producer after the Ivory Coast and Ghana, with 1997 output estimated at 330,000 tonnes, compared with 300,000-310,000 tonnes in 1996.
Malaysia's production is expected to rise marginally to 130,000 tonnes in 1996/97 (October/September) from an estimated 126,000 tonnes the previous season.
A senior Indonesian industry official said that if successful, the cartel could effectively make ASEAN the world's top cocoa producer after the Ivory Coast.

"It has the potential of becoming a producer cartel that can influence international prices," the official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters. "Producers in this region can, to some extent, dictate terms by controlling supply."
But he said there were many issues related to quality, pricing and market share that needed to be ironed out, adding that the plan needed government support if it was to succeed.

"The quality of Malaysian cocoa is much higher than those from Sulawesi, where the bulk of Indonesia's cocoa comes from. How will it be possible for cocoa of differing quality to carry the same pricing?" he asked.
He said that non-ASEAN producers might also take advantage by dumping their cocoa when regional producers hold out for better prices by restricting their supply to the world market.
Malaysian cocoa traders hailed the plan, saying it could have some positive impact on regional prices but doubted if there was enough political will to make it work.
"It's a fact cocoa beans and the industry in Malaysia are now far superior to those in Indonesia, and we have to bridge the gap for such a common pricing plan to work," one said.
